lessons.title: New and Emerging Technologies
lessons.description: How market pull and technology push drive new products and change industry.
lessons.content_html:
What Drives New Technology?

Design and technology does not stand still. Every year, new materials, manufacturing methods and digital tools change the products we use and the way designers work. Understanding why new technologies emerge is as important as knowing what they are. Two key forces drive technological change: market pull and technology push.

Market Pull

Market pull happens when consumers want something that does not yet exist, or want an existing product to work better. The demand comes first; designers and engineers then create a solution. A clear example is the growth of electric vehicles. Public concern about air quality and fossil fuel costs created strong consumer demand for cleaner transport long before carmakers had perfected battery technology. Manufacturers responded by investing heavily in development because the market was pulling them towards the solution.

Market pull is closely linked to the product life cycle. When a product reaches maturity or decline, consumer demand for something better creates a new pull. Smartphone makers release updated handsets annually partly because consumers expect incremental improvements — better cameras, longer battery life, faster processors. This demand is the market pulling the next iteration into existence.

Key Fact

Market pull means consumer or societal demand drives the development of a new product. The market need exists before the product is created.

Technology Push

Technology push works in the opposite direction. Scientists or engineers make a discovery or develop a new capability, and this creates products that consumers did not know they needed. The touchscreen was developed through research into capacitive materials before the first smartphone existed. Once the technology was ready, designers built products around it — consumers then discovered they wanted it.

Dyson’s cyclonic vacuum technology is a well-known example of technology push. James Dyson developed the cyclonic separation principle — using centrifugal force to spin dust out of an airstream without a bag — and then built a product around it. Consumers had not asked for a bagless vacuum; the technology created the market opportunity.

Additive manufacturing — commonly called 3D printing — is a clear case of technology push. Fused deposition modelling (FDM) was developed in the late 1980s for industrial prototyping. Consumers had no concept of printing physical objects at home. As the technology matured and costs fell, desktop 3D printers became available to schools, small businesses and hobbyists. The technology pushed itself into new markets that had not previously existed. Today, 3D printing is used in aerospace (Airbus uses additive manufacturing for lightweight aircraft components), medicine and consumer goods. This shows how a technology push in one industry can ripple into many others.

Consumer Choice and the Global Market

Modern consumers can buy products from anywhere in the world, which affects how designers work. Global production means a single product might be designed in one country, manufactured using components from several others, and sold worldwide. This creates both opportunities and responsibilities. Lower production costs in some regions allow more people to access well-designed products. However, global supply chains also raise questions about workers’ rights, fair wages and environmental standards.

Consumer choice is also shaped by legislation — laws that set standards for safety, energy efficiency and environmental impact. Regulations such as minimum energy performance standards for appliances mean that designers must meet legal requirements, not just consumer preferences. Legislation can therefore act as an additional driver of technological change, pushing manufacturers to develop cleaner or safer products.

Key Fact

Legislation sets minimum standards that products must meet — for example, safety regulations, energy efficiency rules and restrictions on hazardous materials. This forces designers to innovate even when there is no direct consumer demand for change.

Moral, Ethical and Cultural Factors

Technology does not exist in a vacuum. New products raise moral and ethical questions that designers must consider. Planned obsolescence — designing products to have a limited lifespan so consumers buy replacements — generates profit but also waste. Many consumers now actively consider the environmental and ethical record of the brands they buy from, pushing companies to adopt more responsible practices.

Apple’s approach to industrial design under Jonathan Ive became a case study in using aesthetics and material quality to command premium pricing, shaping consumer expectations across the electronics industry. At the same time, Apple’s supply chain practices were scrutinised for working conditions in factories, highlighting the ethical dimension of global production.

A common exam error is writing vague statements such as “make the product more eco-friendly.” Examiners look for specific, actionable improvements — for example, “replace virgin polymer components with recycled HDPE to reduce resource extraction” or “design for disassembly so materials can be separated and recycled at end of life.” The more precise and technically grounded the suggestion, the higher the mark. This applies equally to questions about new technologies — always name a specific technology and explain how it achieves the benefit, not just that it “helps the environment.”

The Product Life Cycle and Enterprise

The product life cycle moves through introduction, growth, maturity and decline. New and emerging technologies extend product life cycles by enabling redesign and improvement. Modular electronics, for instance, let manufacturers update components rather than replace entire devices. This has implications for enterprise — businesses must constantly monitor where their products sit in the life cycle and invest in the next generation before current products reach decline.

Emerging technologies also create new enterprise opportunities. Crowdfunding platforms now allow small designers to test market pull before committing to full-scale manufacture. If a product concept attracts enough backers, the designer has evidence of demand before spending on tooling or materials. This lowers the risk of bringing a new technology to market.
lessons.exam_tip_html: When a question asks you to ‘explain’ the impact of a new technology, always identify whether it is driven by market pull or technology push — then give a named example and explain the consequence for industry or consumers. For extended writing, avoid phrases like “it helps the environment” and instead specify the action: “replacing fossil-fuel-derived nylon with recycled polyester reduces landfill waste and carbon emissions.” Examiners award marks for precision, not for broad claims.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Market pull means consumer demand drives new product development; technology push means a scientific advance creates new product opportunities. Both forces shape the products we use every day.
  • Global production lowers costs but raises ethical questions about workers’ rights and environmental standards — legislation sets minimum standards designers must meet.
  • The product life cycle (introduction → growth → maturity → decline) helps businesses decide when to invest in new technology. Vague sustainability claims in the exam earn no marks — always name a specific action.

lessons.title: Sustainability and the 6 Rs
lessons.description: The 6 Rs framework, Life Cycle Analysis, carbon footprint and fair trade in design.
lessons.content_html:
Why Sustainability Matters in Design

Every product a designer creates uses resources, energy and often generates waste. Sustainability means designing products that minimise their long-term impact on people and the planet. For designers, this is not just an ethical choice — it is increasingly a commercial and legal requirement. The 6 Rs framework gives designers a practical checklist for evaluating how sustainable a product or design decision really is.

The 6 Rs

Rethink: Question whether the product is needed at all, or whether the same function could be achieved with a fundamentally different approach. A designer might rethink a single-use plastic bottle by asking whether a reusable alternative would serve the same need.

Refuse: Decline to use materials or processes that are harmful or unnecessary. This might mean refusing to specify a toxic surface finish when a water-based alternative is available, or refusing to over-package a product when the design can protect itself without additional layers.

Reduce: Use less material, energy and packaging without compromising function. Reducing the wall thickness of an injection-moulded polymer component saves material and speeds up cooling time in the mould, cutting both cost and energy use.

Reuse: Design products and components so they can be used again. Reusable glass bottles, modular electronics, and standardised screw fittings that transfer between products all extend useful life without reprocessing.

Recycle: Ensure materials can be separated and reprocessed at end of life. Marking polymer components with their material code (e.g. HDPE, PP) enables correct sorting at recycling facilities. Designing for disassembly — using screws rather than adhesive bonds — makes this practical.

Repair: Design products that can be fixed rather than discarded. Replacing proprietary fixings with standard screws, providing service manuals, and ensuring spare parts are available all extend a product’s working life. The ‘right to repair’ movement has led to new legislation in some markets requiring manufacturers to supply spare parts for at least several years after a model is discontinued.

Key Fact

The 6 Rs are: Rethink, Refuse, Reduce, Reuse, Recycle, Repair. Examiners look for specific design actions (e.g. “use recycled HDPE pellets”) not vague claims (e.g. “make it greener”).

Life Cycle Analysis

Life Cycle Analysis (LCA) maps every stage of a product’s life: extracting raw materials, processing, manufacturing, distribution, use and end-of-life disposal. At each stage, designers can identify where the largest environmental impacts occur and target improvements there.

Consider a cotton T-shirt. The growing of conventional cotton uses large quantities of water and pesticides — this is where its greatest environmental impact often lies, not in the manufacturing or distribution stage. An LCA reveals this, allowing a designer to specify organic cotton or recycled polyester as a more sustainable alternative. Without LCA, a designer might focus effort on packaging (a small part of the impact) and miss the much larger upstream issue.

A full LCA has four stages: (1) Raw material extraction — mining, logging, petroleum refining; (2) Manufacturing — energy and water used in production, waste generated; (3) Use phase — energy consumed during a product’s working life (often the largest impact for appliances); (4) End of life — whether materials are landfilled, incinerated, recycled or composted. For exam questions, identifying which stage has the greatest impact — and why — is more valuable than just listing all four stages.

Carbon Footprint and Ecological Footprint

A product’s carbon footprint measures the greenhouse gas emissions associated with all stages of its life. It is measured in kilograms of CO₂ equivalent (kg CO₂e). A product’s ecological footprint is broader — it measures the total area of productive land and water needed to produce the resources used and absorb the waste generated.

Designers can reduce a product’s carbon footprint in several specific ways: specifying materials with lower embodied energy (e.g. recycled aluminium requires roughly 95% less energy to produce than primary aluminium from bauxite), reducing transport distances by sourcing materials locally, and designing products to consume less energy in the use phase.

Key Fact

Recycled aluminium requires approximately 95% less energy to produce than primary aluminium smelted from bauxite ore. This makes material choice one of the most powerful tools a designer has for reducing a product’s carbon footprint.

Fair Trade and Social Responsibility

Sustainability is not only environmental — it is also social. Fair trade certification ensures that producers in developing countries receive a fair price for their materials, safe working conditions and community investment. When designers specify fair-trade cotton or certified timber, they are making a social sustainability decision as well as an environmental one.

Cultural responsibility in design means being aware of how a product’s imagery, materials and manufacturing locations affect communities. Designers working on global products must consider whether their choices exploit or support the communities involved in production.

Designing for disassembly is one of the most practical ways to support both repair and recycling. It means: using standard screw fixings rather than adhesive or ultrasonic welding; avoiding mixed-material sandwich constructions where different materials cannot be separated; marking all polymer components with the correct recycling symbol; and providing documentation that allows a service technician (or the user) to take the product apart safely. A product that takes longer to assemble but can be fully disassembled in minutes represents better sustainable design than one that assembles quickly but must be sent to landfill when it fails.
lessons.exam_tip_html: When answering sustainability questions, always replace vague phrases with specific design actions. ‘Make it more eco-friendly’ earns no marks; ‘specify recycled HDPE pellets to reduce virgin polymer use’ or ‘design for disassembly using standard M4 screws instead of adhesive bonding’ earn marks. For LCA questions, identify which stage has the biggest impact and why — don’t just list all four stages. For fair trade, link it explicitly to social sustainability, not just environmental impact.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • The 6 Rs (Rethink, Refuse, Reduce, Reuse, Recycle, Repair) give designers a practical framework for making sustainable choices — always support each R with a specific design action, not a vague claim.
  • Life Cycle Analysis maps environmental impact across all stages of a product’s life, helping designers target where improvements matter most — often raw material extraction or the use phase, not just packaging.
  • Carbon footprint, ecological footprint, and fair trade are all dimensions of sustainability. Recycled aluminium uses roughly 95% less energy than primary aluminium — material selection is one of the most powerful levers designers have.

lessons.title: Energy Generation and Storage
lessons.description: Renewable and non-renewable energy sources, fossil fuels, and how products store energy.
lessons.content_html:
Energy in Design and Technology

Every product requires energy to manufacture, and many require energy to use. Designers must understand where energy comes from and how it is stored, because these choices affect a product’s sustainability, cost and practicality. Energy sources fall into two broad categories: renewable energy and non-renewable energy.

Renewable Energy Sources

Solar (photovoltaic): Photovoltaic (PV) cells convert sunlight directly into electricity. Silicon-based PV cells are the most common. Solar panels on buildings and integrated into products (calculators, garden lights) reduce dependence on mains power. Efficiency of commercially available panels typically ranges from around 15–22% for silicon cells.

Wind: Wind turbines use the kinetic energy of moving air to spin a generator. Onshore turbines are cheaper to build and maintain; offshore turbines benefit from stronger and more consistent winds. Wind power is intermittent — output depends on wind speed — so energy storage is needed to smooth supply.

Hydroelectric: Water flowing through a turbine — usually in a dam — generates electricity. Hydroelectric power is reliable and controllable, but requires a suitable geographical location and raises environmental concerns about the habitat flooded by reservoirs.

Geothermal: Heat from the Earth’s crust is used to generate steam that drives turbines or to heat buildings directly. Practically available in regions with volcanic activity, such as Iceland, but less so in the UK.

Biomass: Organic material — wood, crop waste, dedicated energy crops — is burned or fermented to release energy. It is considered low-carbon (the CO₂ released was recently absorbed by the growing plant), but combustion still produces particulates and other pollutants.

Wave and tidal: The movement of ocean waves and tidal flows can drive turbines. The UK’s coastal location makes these sources potentially significant, but the technology is less mature and more expensive than wind or solar at present.

Key Fact

The six main renewable energy sources covered in this course are: solar, wind, hydroelectric, geothermal, biomass, and wave/tidal. All are replenished naturally, but most are intermittent or location-dependent — requiring storage or grid balancing to be practically useful.

Non-Renewable Energy Sources

Fossil fuels — coal, oil and natural gas — were formed over millions of years from the remains of ancient organisms. Burning them releases the carbon stored in them as CO₂, contributing to the greenhouse effect and climate change. They are energy-dense and have well-established distribution infrastructure, which is why they still supply the majority of global energy.

Nuclear power is sometimes described as ‘low carbon’ because it does not burn fuel. Uranium atoms are split in a process called fission, releasing large amounts of heat used to generate steam and electricity. Nuclear power produces a reliable baseload of electricity without direct CO₂ emissions, but generates radioactive waste that must be stored safely for thousands of years, and carries a small risk of catastrophic accidents.

The following table compares key characteristics:

Feature Fossil fuels Renewables (e.g. solar/wind)
AvailabilityFinite; will run outContinuously replenished
CO₂ emissionsHighLow to zero during operation
ReliabilityOn-demand (energy-dense)Often intermittent (wind/solar)
InfrastructureWell-establishedExpanding rapidly

Energy Storage for Products and Manufacturing

Many products need to store energy so they can be used without a permanent connection to the mains. The main storage methods are:

Batteries are the most common energy storage for portable products. Rechargeable lithium-ion batteries power smartphones, laptops and electric vehicles because of their high energy density and long cycle life. Non-rechargeable alkaline batteries are used in lower-drain products such as TV remotes. Battery disposal is an environmental concern — lithium and other metals require specialist recycling.

Mains electricity powers most manufacturing equipment and large household appliances. It is reliable and effectively unlimited in supply, but the carbon intensity of the grid depends on how the electricity was generated — a factory powered by renewable electricity has a lower carbon footprint than one on coal-sourced power.

Wind-up mechanisms store mechanical energy in a spring. Traditionally used in clockwork mechanisms and wind-up toys, they are now applied in products for regions without reliable electricity — such as wind-up radios and torches designed for off-grid use in developing countries. The Freeplay wind-up radio is a well-known example of this approach applied for social good.

Key Fact

Lithium-ion batteries are preferred for portable and high-drain applications because of their high energy density (they store a lot of energy per unit of weight) and long cycle life (they can be recharged hundreds or thousands of times). Alkaline batteries have lower energy density and cannot be recharged.

PV cells can be integrated directly into products to provide power without batteries or mains connection. Applications include: solar-powered calculators (very low power draw — even indoor light is sufficient); garden lighting (PV cell charges a battery during the day, powers LEDs at night); and building-integrated PV panels on roofs and facades. In wearable technology, flexible thin-film PV cells are being embedded into clothing and backpack fabric, though efficiency remains lower than rigid silicon cells. The key design consideration is surface area: PV cells must be exposed to light, which affects the form and orientation of the product.
lessons.exam_tip_html: Energy questions often ask you to ‘compare’ or ‘discuss’ renewable and non-renewable sources. Always link each source to a specific advantage and limitation — for example, solar is clean and silent but intermittent; nuclear is reliable and low-carbon but produces radioactive waste. For storage questions, name the storage method and explain why it suits the product: ‘a lithium-ion battery is used because of its high energy density, allowing the device to operate for many hours without recharging.’
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Renewable energy sources (solar, wind, hydroelectric, geothermal, biomass, wave/tidal) are replenished naturally but are often intermittent; non-renewable sources (coal, oil, gas, nuclear) are energy-dense but finite or produce problematic waste.
  • Photovoltaic cells convert sunlight to electricity and can be integrated into products; lithium-ion batteries provide high energy density for portable and high-drain applications; wind-up mechanisms store mechanical energy for off-grid use.
  • In the exam, always link each energy source to a specific advantage and a real limitation — and link each storage method to why it suits the product it powers.

lessons.title: Smart Materials and Modern Materials
lessons.description: SMA, polymorph, thermo-chromic, electroluminescent film, QTC and phase-changing materials.
lessons.content_html:
What Are Smart Materials?

Smart materials change one of their own properties in response to an environmental stimulus. This response is predictable and usually reversible: remove the stimulus and the material returns to its original state. Smart materials are increasingly used in product design because they can replace complex mechanical components with a simpler, lighter and more responsive material solution.

Shape Memory Alloy (SMA)

Shape memory alloy (SMA) is a metal — typically a nickel–titanium alloy called nitinol — that can be deformed when cool and then returns to its original shape when heated above its transition temperature. This behaviour is useful in medical devices: SMA stents are inserted into blood vessels in a compressed form and then expand to the correct diameter when warmed by body heat, without requiring a mechanical inflation device.

In consumer products, SMA wire is used in eyeglass frames that spring back after being bent, and in thermostatic valves that open automatically when temperature rises. The key examiner point is that SMA is a metal with a recoverable change — not a polymer — and the change requires heat above a specific transition temperature.

Key Fact

Shape memory alloy (SMA) is typically a nickel–titanium alloy (nitinol). It can be deformed when cold and returns to its original shape when heated above its transition temperature. Applications include medical stents, self-straightening eyeglass frames and thermostatic valves.

Polymorph

Polymorph is a thermoplastic material supplied as small white pellets. It becomes soft and mouldable when placed in warm water (approximately 62°C) and can be shaped by hand. When it cools to room temperature it becomes rigid and white. It can be reheated and reshaped repeatedly. Designers use polymorph for rapid prototyping and for creating custom-fit components — for example, custom grips for tools or orthopaedic supports shaped directly to a user’s body.

Thermo-chromic Materials

Thermo-chromic materials change colour when heated or cooled. The colour change is reversible — cool the material down and the original colour returns. They are used in thermometers (the liquid crystal type that changes colour across a temperature range), on baby feeding spoons (indicating when food is too hot), and in novelty mugs and packaging that reveal a graphic when a hot drink is poured in.

Photo-chromic materials change colour in response to light — specifically ultraviolet (UV) radiation. The most familiar application is self-tinting (photochromic) spectacle lenses, which darken outdoors and lighten indoors. Photo-chromic inks are used in security printing and on some packaging to indicate UV exposure.

Key Fact

Thermo-chromic materials respond to temperature; photo-chromic materials respond to light (UV). Both changes are reversible. Common exam error: confusing the stimulus for each type.

Electroluminescent Film

Electroluminescent (EL) film emits light when an electrical current passes through it. The film is thin, flexible and can be produced in large sheets or cut to shape. Applications include: illuminated safety clothing and cycle jackets, backlighting for instrument panels, and low-power decorative lighting in wearable technology. Because it is thin and flexible, EL film can be incorporated into textiles and clothing designs that would not accommodate conventional LED strips.

Quantum Tunnelling Composite (QTC)

Quantum tunnelling composite (QTC) is a flexible, rubber-like material that is normally an electrical insulator. When compressed, conductive metal particles within the material are forced close enough together to allow electrons to ‘tunnel’ through the gaps, making the material conduct electricity. The resistance drops dramatically — and controllably — with pressure. QTC is used in touch-sensitive gloves for touchscreen operation, in pressure sensors for medical devices, and in on/off switches that require no mechanical moving parts.

Modern materials include engineered composites that combine the best properties of two or more constituent materials. Carbon fibre reinforced polymer (CFRP) combines carbon fibre strands (very high stiffness and tensile strength) with a polymer matrix (typically epoxy resin) that binds the fibres and protects them. CFRP is used in aircraft frames, racing car bodies and high-performance bicycle frames because it is stiffer and lighter than steel. Kevlar (para-aramid fibre) is extremely tough and used in body armour, cut-resistant gloves and helmets. Glass-reinforced plastic (GRP) uses glass fibre in a polyester or epoxy resin matrix; it is cheaper than CFRP and used for boat hulls, car body panels and storage tanks. These materials are covered in more depth in the Composites and Technical Textiles lesson.

Phase-Changing Materials

Phase-changing materials (PCMs) absorb large amounts of heat as they melt (change from solid to liquid) and release that heat as they solidify. This behaviour is used in building insulation, packaging for temperature-sensitive pharmaceuticals, and in specialist clothing — where PCM microcapsules embedded in fabric absorb body heat when the wearer is active and release it when the wearer cools down, helping to regulate body temperature.

Nomex and Rhovyl

Nomex is a heat-resistant para-aramid fibre used in protective clothing for firefighters, racing drivers and military personnel. It does not melt or drip when exposed to flame, which prevents the fabric sticking to skin. Rhovyl is a chlorofibre derived from polyvinyl chloride (PVC). It has naturally flame-retardant properties and is used in protective nightwear and bedding, particularly for young children and elderly people. Both are specialist performance fibres rather than general-purpose textiles.

A frequent error is describing thermo-chromic materials as responding to light, or photo-chromic materials as responding to heat. The names contain the clue: ‘thermo’ = heat, ‘photo’ = light. Similarly, students sometimes describe SMA as ‘growing’ or ‘expanding’ when it should be described as ‘returning to its pre-set shape.’ The material does not expand arbitrarily — it returns to one specific memorised geometry. For QTC, the key point is that it is insulating under no pressure but conducts under compression — stating this contrast earns the mark.
lessons.exam_tip_html: For smart materials questions, always state the stimulus (what causes the change) and the response (what changes). Thermo-chromic: stimulus = temperature change; response = colour change. Photo-chromic: stimulus = UV light; response = colour change. SMA: stimulus = heat above transition temperature; response = returns to pre-set shape. QTC: stimulus = pressure/compression; response = changes from insulator to conductor. For extended writing on smart materials, include a specific application and explain why that material’s properties make it suitable for that context.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Smart materials respond predictably and reversibly to a stimulus: SMA to heat (returns to pre-set shape), thermo-chromic to temperature (colour change), photo-chromic to UV light (colour change), QTC to pressure (insulator to conductor), EL film to electricity (emits light).
  • Modern materials include composites (CFRP, Kevlar, GRP), phase-changing materials (absorb/release heat on melting/solidifying), and specialist fibres like Nomex (flame-resistant) and Rhovyl (chlorofibre, flame-retardant).
  • In exam answers, always name the stimulus and the response for each smart material — and link the application to why that specific property is useful in that product or context.

lessons.title: Composites and Technical Textiles
lessons.description: Carbon fibre, Kevlar, GRP, geotextiles, micro-fibres and wearable textile electronics.
lessons.content_html:
What Are Composite Materials?

Composite materials are engineered by combining two or more different materials. One material acts as the reinforcement (providing strength or stiffness) and the other acts as the matrix (binding the reinforcement together and protecting it). Neither component alone has all the properties of the finished composite. This is why composites can outperform conventional metals or polymers for specific applications.

Carbon Fibre Reinforced Polymer (CFRP)

Carbon fibre reinforced polymer (CFRP) combines carbon fibre strands with a polymer matrix — typically epoxy resin. Carbon fibres are made by heating polyacrylonitrile (PAN) at high temperatures in a controlled atmosphere until most non-carbon atoms are driven off, leaving a fibre that is almost pure carbon. These fibres have very high tensile strength and stiffness but are brittle on their own. The epoxy resin matrix binds the fibres, distributes loads between them and protects them from impact and chemical attack.

CFRP is significantly lighter than steel for the same structural strength, making it essential in applications where weight saving is critical. Airbus uses CFRP extensively in modern commercial aircraft — the wings and fuselage sections of aircraft such as the A350 are predominantly CFRP, reducing aircraft weight and therefore fuel consumption per passenger. It is also used in Formula 1 monocoques, high-performance bicycle frames and sporting equipment.

Key Fact

CFRP has a very high strength-to-weight ratio — it is stiffer and stronger than steel by weight, while being significantly lighter. This property is why Airbus uses it in aircraft structures, reducing fuel consumption. Its disadvantages include high manufacturing cost and difficulty of repair after impact damage.

Kevlar (Para-Aramid Fibre)

Kevlar is a synthetic para-aramid fibre developed by DuPont. It has exceptionally high tensile strength — around five times stronger than steel by weight — and outstanding toughness (resistance to tearing and impact). Unlike CFRP, Kevlar is not brittle; it absorbs energy by deforming rather than shattering. This makes it the preferred material for personal protective equipment: body armour (bullet-resistant vests), cut-resistant gloves for food processing and industrial use, and motorcycle protective clothing.

Kevlar is also used as reinforcement in composite structures where impact resistance is important — for example, in the hulls of racing kayaks and in aerospace structures where bird-strike resistance is required. It can be combined with carbon fibre in a hybrid composite to balance stiffness (from CFRP) with toughness (from Kevlar).

Glass-Reinforced Plastic (GRP)

Glass-reinforced plastic (GRP) uses glass fibre as the reinforcement within a polyester or epoxy resin matrix. It is cheaper and easier to manufacture than CFRP. GRP is corrosion-resistant, mouldable into complex shapes and has a good strength-to-weight ratio (though lower than CFRP). It is used for boat hulls, surf and kayak shells, car body panels (notably on classic sports cars), storage tanks and low-cost architectural cladding panels.

The table below compares the three main composites:

Material Reinforcement Key property Typical use
CFRPCarbon fibreVery high stiffness and strength-to-weightAircraft structures, racing cars
Kevlar (KFRP)Para-aramid fibreVery high toughness and impact resistanceBody armour, cut-resistant gloves
GRPGlass fibreGood strength-to-weight, corrosion-resistant, lower costBoat hulls, car panels, tanks

Technical Textiles

Technical textiles are designed for performance rather than appearance. They are engineered to meet specific requirements in demanding applications: protection, filtration, moisture management or structural reinforcement.

Geotextiles

Geotextiles are permeable fabrics used in civil engineering. They are laid in the ground to separate, filter, reinforce or drain soil. A road built over soft ground may have a geotextile layer between the sub-soil and the gravel base to prevent mixing while still allowing water to drain through. Geotextiles are typically made from polypropylene or polyester and are produced in woven or non-woven forms depending on the required balance of strength and permeability.

Micro-Fibres

Micro-fibres are synthetic fibres with a diameter of less than one denier — finer than a strand of silk. The fine structure creates a very dense weave with billions of tiny air pockets, making micro-fibre fabrics soft, lightweight and highly effective at moisture management. They are used in sports clothing (wicking away sweat to keep athletes dry and comfortable), in microfibre cleaning cloths (the fine fibres mechanically trap dirt and bacteria without needing chemical cleaners), and in waterproof breathable membranes.

Interactive and Wearable Textile Electronics

Wearable electronics embed electronic functionality into textiles without making them rigid or unwearable. Methods include: weaving conductive metallic yarns into fabric to create circuits; attaching flexible printed circuit boards to the textile; and integrating sensors, LEDs or heating elements directly into clothing. Applications include: sports performance garments with heart rate and motion sensors; heated motorcycle and ski clothing; and electroluminescent safety vests for cyclists and construction workers.

The key challenge in wearable electronics is durability — the electronics must survive washing, stretching and the mechanical stresses of wear. Encapsulation (covering components in a flexible protective coating) and careful choice of washable conductive materials are the main technical solutions.

Key Fact

Technical textiles covered in this unit include geotextiles (civil engineering — road and drainage), micro-fibres (sports clothing and cleaning), breathable membranes (outdoor gear), and interactive textiles (wearable electronics in sports and safety garments).

Breathable membranes such as PTFE (polytetrafluoroethylene) expanded membranes work by having pores large enough to allow water vapour (sweat) to escape but small enough to block liquid water droplets. This one-way passage makes the fabric waterproof while remaining breathable. Moisture management fabrics use capillary action: a hydrophobic inner layer (repelling liquid water) sits against the skin and pushes moisture outward into a hydrophilic outer layer that spreads it over a wide surface area for rapid evaporation. Sun-protective clothing uses tightly woven or coated fabrics with a UV Protection Factor (UPF) rating, blocking UV radiation from reaching the skin.
lessons.exam_tip_html: For questions comparing composites, always name the reinforcement and matrix materials, not just the composite. ‘CFRP uses carbon fibre in an epoxy resin matrix’ is more creditworthy than ‘carbon fibre is strong and light.’ For technical textiles questions, link the fabric structure to the function it achieves — for example, ‘micro-fibre’s very fine diameter creates billions of tiny air pockets that trap dirt mechanically without chemicals.’ Always name at least one specific application when the question asks you to explain why a material is suitable.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Composites combine a reinforcement (e.g. carbon, glass or aramid fibre) with a matrix (e.g. epoxy resin) to achieve properties neither component has alone. CFRP is used in aircraft (Airbus) for its stiffness-to-weight ratio; Kevlar provides toughness for body armour; GRP is the lower-cost option for boat hulls and car panels.
  • Technical textiles are engineered for performance: geotextiles for civil engineering, micro-fibres for moisture management, breathable membranes for waterproof-breathable clothing, and interactive textiles for wearable electronics in sports and safety applications.
  • In exam answers, name the reinforcement and matrix for composites, and link the fabric structure to the specific function it achieves for technical textiles.

lessons.title: CAD, CAM and Production Techniques
lessons.description: CAD and CAM advantages and disadvantages, CNC routing, laser cutting and 3D printing.
lessons.content_html:
Digital Design and Manufacture

Computer-aided design and computer-aided manufacture have transformed how products move from concept to production. Computer-Aided Design (CAD) allows designers to model products precisely on-screen, test their appearance and function digitally, and generate the files needed to control manufacturing machinery. Computer-Aided Manufacture (CAM) takes those files and uses them to directly control machine tools, removing the need for a skilled operator to set up every cut or movement manually.

Together, CAD and CAM form a workflow that can take a product from initial sketch to finished part with very high precision and repeatability. This does not mean they replace skilled designers — the creativity and judgement of the designer remain essential — but they do change what skills are most valued in modern manufacturing.

Advantages of CAD

CAD software allows designers to create two-dimensional drawings and three-dimensional solid models that can be rotated, sectioned and rendered to look like the finished product. Changes to one dimension automatically update the whole model, eliminating the redrawing required in manual draughting. Designers can simulate how a structure will behave under load (Finite Element Analysis), check whether moving parts will clash before any physical prototype is made, and share files instantly with manufacturers or clients anywhere in the world.

CAD also enables rapid prototyping: a 3D model can be exported directly to a 3D printer or CNC machine within minutes of completion. The file is the product specification, reducing the chance of errors introduced by verbal or written instructions. Multiple iterations of a design can be tested digitally at almost no cost before expensive physical prototyping begins.

Key Fact

Key CAD advantages: designs can be modified instantly and shared globally; simulations can test structural performance before manufacture; files can be output directly to CAM machines, reducing manual error. Key disadvantage: high software cost and significant training time required before productivity improves.

Disadvantages of CAD

CAD software licences are expensive — professional packages such as AutoCAD or SolidWorks can cost thousands of pounds per seat per year. Hardware must be powerful enough to handle large assemblies without lag. Training staff to use CAD competently takes significant time, and there is a risk of over-reliance on the software: designers who cannot sketch or think in 3D without a computer lose problem-solving flexibility.

There is also a security risk: digital design files can be copied and shared, creating potential intellectual property problems. A factory that loses its server, or a design studio that is subject to a cyberattack, may lose access to years of design data if backup protocols are not in place.

Advantages of CAM

CAM-controlled machines can run 24 hours a day without rest, producing identical parts every cycle. This consistency is impossible to match with hand-operated tools, where operator fatigue introduces variation over time. Complex shapes that would take a skilled machinist hours to produce manually can be cut automatically from a CAD file. This is especially important for three-dimensional contoured surfaces in product design and for fine detail work in jewellery and signage.

CNC (computer numerical control) machines coordinate movement across multiple axes — typically X, Y and Z — to produce precise, complex geometries. Once programmed, a CNC machine can produce identical parts in batch quantities without further operator intervention. Waste is reduced because the toolpath can be optimised to minimise material removal.

Key Fact

CAM reduces waste in two ways: toolpaths can be optimised by software to minimise material removed (nesting patterns on sheet material), and the consistency of machine operation means fewer rejected parts due to operator error. This makes CAM particularly cost-effective for batch and mass production.

Disadvantages of CAM

CAM equipment has very high capital costs. A CNC milling machine or laser cutter suitable for industry costs tens of thousands of pounds. Set-up time is significant: programming the toolpath and fixturing the workpiece correctly requires skilled technicians. For one-off or very small batch production, the time and cost of set-up may exceed the time it would take a skilled craftsperson to make the part manually.

When a CAM machine breaks down, production stops entirely unless a spare machine is available — a single point of failure that does not exist in a workshop where multiple skilled workers can redistribute tasks. Maintenance requires specialist engineers who command high salaries.

CNC Routing and Laser Cutting

CNC routing uses a rotating bit to cut, carve and shape flat sheet materials — typically wood, MDF, acrylic and soft metals. The router head moves across the bed following the CAD file toolpath. It is widely used in furniture manufacture, signage and architectural models. CNC routing can produce complex interlocking joints and relief carving that would be impractical by hand in batch quantities.

Laser cutting uses a focused beam of high-energy light to cut or engrave flat sheet materials with extreme precision. Acrylic, wood, card, fabric and thin sheet metal can all be cut without physical contact, meaning no blade wear and no cutting forces that might distort delicate pieces. The kerf (cut width) is typically less than 0.5 mm. Laser cutting is used in schools and small workshops for model-making, in industry for precision sheet metal parts, and in the jewellery and fashion industries for intricate fabric and leather cutting. A significant advantage is the ability to nest many parts tightly on one sheet, minimising material waste.

CNC embroidery and vinyl cutting extend CAM principles to textiles and graphics: embroidery machines follow a digitised pattern to stitch designs into fabric precisely and repeatedly; vinyl cutters trace vector paths to cut self-adhesive vinyl for signage, vehicle graphics and garment decoration. Both processes produce consistent, high-quality results at speeds impossible to match by hand.

3D Printing (Additive Manufacturing)

3D printing builds parts by adding material layer by layer, rather than removing material as CNC machines do. The most common process is Fused Deposition Modelling (FDM): a thermoplastic filament (typically PLA or ABS) is heated and extruded through a nozzle, depositing each layer on the build platform until the part is complete. This allows complex internal geometries — hollow sections, internal channels — that are impossible to produce by subtractive machining.

Other processes include Stereolithography (SLA), which cures liquid resin with a UV laser to build very fine-detail parts, and Selective Laser Sintering (SLS), which fuses polymer or metal powder with a laser and is suitable for production-grade engineering parts without support material. Airbus uses metal SLS to produce titanium brackets and connectors for aircraft cabins — components that would be difficult and wasteful to machine from solid billet.

Advantages: complex geometries at no extra tooling cost; no fixed tooling means economical one-off production; rapid iteration of design without new moulds; can produce personalised or bespoke parts directly from a digital file. Disadvantages: slow build speed compared with injection moulding for large batches; FDM parts have visible layer lines and may require surface finishing; material choice is narrower than conventional manufacturing; parts may be weaker along the layer boundaries than in the in-plane direction (anisotropic strength).

Students sometimes describe ‘CAD’ when they mean the machine cutting the part, or ‘CAM’ when they mean the drawing software. Keep them distinct: CAD is the design tool (the computer screen, the modelling software, the drawing or simulation); CAM is the manufacturing tool (the CNC machine, the laser cutter, the 3D printer). The CAD file is the input; the CAM process is the output. For exam questions, specify both the design tool and the manufacturing machine — e.g. ‘the designer creates the part in CAD software, then outputs a DXF file to a laser cutter (CAM) which cuts the acrylic sheet.’
lessons.exam_tip_html: For ‘discuss advantages and disadvantages’ questions on CAD or CAM, write developed points — not just a list. Each point should name the feature and explain the benefit or drawback in context: ‘CAM machines run 24 hours without fatigue, producing identical parts every cycle, which is impossible to match with hand tools over a long shift.’ For questions comparing CNC routing, laser cutting and 3D printing, always name at least one suitable material for each process and one context where it is preferred. Avoid confusing CAD (design software) with CAM (manufacturing machine).
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • CAD creates precise digital models that can be modified instantly and output directly to manufacturing machinery; CAM uses those files to control machine tools for consistent, repeatable production. Both have significant software/hardware costs and training demands.
  • CNC routing shapes flat sheet material using rotating bits; laser cutting uses a focused light beam for precise, contactless cutting of wood, acrylic and fabric; 3D printing builds parts additively layer by layer (FDM, SLA or SLS) enabling complex internal geometries impossible by subtractive methods.
  • In exam answers, always distinguish CAD from CAM, name materials suited to each process, and explain why each process suits its application — e.g. laser cutting is chosen for fine detail and minimal kerf; 3D printing for one-off complex geometries with no tooling cost.

practice_questions.marks:
One mark per disadvantage (any two):

• Significant training time required before productivity improves
• Requires powerful and expensive hardware

[2 marks]

practice_questions.text: Describe how a laser cutter would be used to produce an acrylic panel for a product prototype.
practice_questions.marks:
Up to 3 marks:
• The acrylic sheet is placed flat on the laser cutter bed (1).
• A vector file (from CAD software) is loaded and the machine is set to the correct power and speed for the material thickness (1).
• The laser beam cuts along the defined paths, producing the panel shape with a very narrow kerf and smooth edges that may require no further finishing (1).
[3 marks]

practice_questions.text: Explain why a designer would choose 3D printing (FDM) rather than CNC routing to produce a one-off prototype of a hollow enclosure for an electronic device.
practice_questions.marks:
2 marks per developed point:
• 3D printing can produce hollow internal geometries directly, whereas CNC routing is limited to surface features and cannot easily create enclosed internal cavities in a single operation (1). This means the enclosure can be built as one piece with a lid and internal ribbing all included in a single print (1).
• 3D printing requires no tooling or fixturing specific to the shape — only the digital file is needed (1). For a one-off prototype, this eliminates the set-up cost and time that a CNC routing operation would require (1).
[4 marks]

practice_questions.text: A school workshop has a budget to purchase one machine for making acrylic and MDF components for GCSE D&T projects. Compare the suitability of a laser cutter and a CNC router for this purpose.
practice_questions.marks:
Award marks for comparative points:
• A laser cutter can cut acrylic and MDF cleanly with a very narrow kerf and no cutting forces, reducing the risk of workpiece distortion or material fracture in thin sheet work (1).
• A CNC router can cut thicker MDF and solid wood that a laser cutter cannot safely process; it is also capable of 3D relief carving, extending what students can make (1).
• A laser cutter can engrave text and patterns onto flat sheet surfaces rapidly, which is useful for design decoration (1).
• Both require CAD files and safety enclosures; the laser cutter requires ventilation for fumes from acrylic and MDF cutting (1).
• For a GCSE workshop focused on flat sheet work, the laser cutter’s precision, minimal kerf and ability to engrave may make it the more versatile choice; for a workshop producing structural 3D woodwork, the CNC router offers greater depth capacity (1).
[5 marks]

practice_questions.text: Discuss the advantages and disadvantages of using CNC manufacturing rather than manual craft production for a batch of 500 identical timber jewellery boxes.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Balanced discussion of CNC advantages (consistency, 24-hour operation, complex joint geometry, reduced operator error, optimised nesting minimises material waste) and disadvantages (high capital cost of machinery, significant set-up and programming time, maintenance requires specialist engineers, single point of failure if machine breaks down, loss of craftsperson skills). Weighted judgement about whether CNC is justified at a batch of 500.
Secure: Two developed advantages and two developed disadvantages with specific context (e.g. nesting, kerf, batch size economics); conclusion present.
Developing: Points mostly listed; limited development; one side stronger.
Emerging: Simple pros/cons; no specific context or judgement.
[8 marks — levels-based]
